blocks.text: Revelation 4 opens a heavenly throne vision. John sees the one seated on the throne, twenty-four elders, flashes of lightning and thunder, seven lamps, a crystal-like sea, and four living creatures. The creatures and elders continually give glory, honor, and thanks, casting their crowns before the throne. The chapter's final confession centers creation: the Lord is worthy because all things were created by his will.

The supplied context places worship within covenant life, temple worship, kingship, wisdom, and prophetic critique. It also describes holiness as ordering both worship and life. Revelation 4's throne-centered scene therefore presents praise, posture, crowns, and repeated acclamation as an ordered response to the holiness and sovereignty of the one seated on the throne.

Revelation repeatedly recomposes imagery associated with Ezekiel—throne, living creatures, and other visionary features—within its own literary sequence. The presence of familiar prophetic imagery should therefore be read as reuse and recomposition, not as a demand that every detail reproduce one earlier vision in a one-to-one way.

Revelation repeatedly reworks Israel's Scriptures, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. The following throne vision presents the slaughtered Lamb as worthy to open the scroll and receive worship, so chapter 4's praise of the Creator prepares for the next scene's expansion of worthiness and worship.

sections.title: The throne vision and the Lamb
